RESPONSE:
# Points from "How We Work", recalled from memory

Exact wording will have drifted in places, and I've flagged the points I'm least sure of.

## Opening

- The note is short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It is written down because ordinary good practice is what slips: under deadline, late in a long day, or when a confident colleague is in the room.

## 1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned

- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries, and your own earlier notes. Each has earned a weight from its evidence, and your job is to hold it at exactly that weight.
- **Not more**, because it is fluent, comes from someone senior, or confirms what you hoped.
- **Not less**, because it is inconvenient, comes from someone junior, or because doubting feels rigorous.
- Ask three questions: what supports it, how directly, and what would have to be true for it to be wrong.
- A well-measured result from a controlled comparison is heavy.
- A plausible mechanism suggested after the data were in is light, but not nothing. Note it and say what would test it.
- A confident sentence carries the weight of its evidence and no more. Confidence is information about the speaker, not about the world.
- Both errors are costly but not equally visible:
  - Inflation is easy to spot afterwards.
  - Deflation is harder. A caveat on a sound result looks careful but is a misreport.
- Hedging a supported claim is as much a distortion as overstating an unsupported one.
- **Example:** a supplier's defect rate fell after a process change.
  - If the evidence is three months of the supplier's own figures, say so and weigh it accordingly.
  - If it is a year of your own incoming inspection, don't bury it under "it may be noise".

## 2. Take in what was said before you answer

- Take in all of a paper, message, or review before responding, and show that you have.
- Restate the substance briefly in your own terms. This is not politeness: it is how both sides find out whether what was received matches what was sent.
- The part you don't restate is the part most likely to drop.
- A reply that handles three easy points and silently skips the hard fourth has answered a different, easier message.
- If you can't restate something, you haven't understood it, and the next move is a question.
- Then move on. The restatement is the ground, not the contribution. The useful part is what your understanding makes available: the implication, the gap, the next test.
- **Example:** a manager's five-point request with the budget question in the middle. Restate all five in a line each, answer four, and say plainly that the budget needs figures you don't yet have and when you'll have them.

## 3. Go to the source

- Summaries, abstracts, notes, and memory are all compressions. Compression loses the details that later matter: the denominator, the subgroup, the condition under which the result held.
- When a decision depends on a specific, check the primary material, not the summary (however good) or your recollection (however confident).
- This applies most to things you think you already know. The claims most likely to have drifted are the ones you've repeated to yourself most often.
- The source is the referee, not agreement among colleagues. A team that checks claims against each other rather than the data can drift together into a shared mistake no one inside can see.
- **Example:** you remember a report as saying "costs fell 12%". It actually said "costs per unit fell 12% while volume fell 20%". Open it before citing it in a budget meeting.

## 4. Don't close what is open, or keep open what is closed

- Mark honestly which questions the evidence settles and which it leaves open, and keep them that way.
- **Closing early** is tempting because it feels like progress: something reportable, a task ticked off. But it turns uncertainty into a false fact that others build on.
  - If a question is open, say so, say what would close it, and carry it forward as open.
- **The mirror error** is keeping a settled question open, because closing it is uncomfortable or one more check feels safer. This wastes effort and signals doubt the evidence doesn't support.
  - Close it, say why, and move on.
- **Example:** a new form reduced errors at two sites. Whether it works at the busiest site, which has a different workflow, is open. Report the first as found and the second as open, not as "promising" and "likely".

## 5. Value the colleague who sees differently

- The most useful thing a colleague offers is what you couldn't produce yourself: an objection from a different starting point, a reading that didn't pass through your assumptions.
- A reviewer who knows exactly what you know mostly returns what you already see. Difference is the source of new information.
- When asking for a check, give the material and the question, not your conclusion, your worries, or what you hope they'll find. Telling them doesn't just bias them; it removes the difference that made them worth asking.
- In reverse: as the fresh reader, read first, form your view, and only then look at what others concluded.
- Raise objections when you have them. An objection held back because the room seems settled is information the team doesn't get.
- *(I don't recall a worked example in this section. I think there wasn't one.)*

## 6. Make your moves where they can be seen

- When you can see the right next step, take it, and make it visible so others can check and reverse it.
  - Share drafts before they feel finished.
  - Make the call and show your reasoning.
  - Push the result so someone can look at it.
- Asking permission for a decision the evidence already settles hands it to someone with less context, and stalls the work on your guess about their answer.
- That guess is your own model of them and contains nothing you didn't already have. Only a real move gets a real reply, and the real reply is where you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This is not licence to ignore others. Moves that are hard to reverse, or that commit other people's time, deserve a conversation first.
- Most moves are reversible, and for those the default is to make them openly.
- **Example:** instead of asking "should I restructure section three?", restructure it in a copy, say what changed and why, and invite reversal.

## 7. Failures come in pairs

Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one tends to push toward the other.
- **Inflating / deflating a claim:** overstating a provisional result vs. hedging a supported one into vagueness.
- **Inventing a flaw / inventing a reassurance:** finding a problem that isn't there to look rigorous vs. dismissing a real one to keep things moving.
- **Closing too early / keeping open too long.**
- **Killing a live line / keeping a dead one:** dropping an idea at the first difficulty vs. persisting with one the evidence has ruled out.
- **Deferring / dismissing:** accepting a claim because of who made it vs. rejecting it for the same reason.
- **Offloading / overriding:** asking others to decide what you can see vs. deciding what genuinely needs their input.

If you catch yourself correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.

## A last word

- The note is not a rulebook to consult at every step. It describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and is mostly carried without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the work itself: the source that overrules you, the colleague who reads differently, the result that doesn't come out as expected.
- Welcome those, because they are how you find out what you didn't already know.
